clue.text: Exotic beard and pigtail seen at a garden-party?

parts.note: 'Exotic' asks for a foreign word: barbe is French for beard
a cue (or queue) is an old word for a pigtail of hair hanging behind

explanation.surface: Someone with an outlandish beard and pigtail turns up at a garden-party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exotic' points to the French word for beard; the old spelling CUE for a pigtail completes it. The question mark marks the definition as an example: an outdoor party with grilled food.
explanation.definitionFit: An outdoor meal with food grilled over charcoal is a kind of party held in a garden.

clue.text: Local bank is away from the trunk line

definitions.meaning: a local office of a bank, as opposed to its head office
a railway line that leaves the main (trunk) line to serve a smaller place

explanation.definitionFit: A local office of a bank and a secondary railway line leaving the main route are both offshoots of a larger body.

clue.text: Canary that keeps a level pitch

definitions.meaning: a breed of canary known for its rolling song
a heavy cylinder used to flatten a cricket pitch

explanation.walkthrough: 'Canary' and 'level pitch' suggest a singer holding a note, but the pitch is a cricket pitch kept flat by a heavy cylinder drawn over it.
explanation.definitionFit: A breed of canary takes its name from its trilling song, and the groundsman's heavy cylinder flattens a cricket pitch.

clue.text: A bit of old Italy in the Potteries

definitions.meaning: the ancient region of the Etruscans in central Italy
Josiah Wedgwood named his works and village near Stoke-on-Trent after the ancient Italian region

explanation.walkthrough: The Potteries is the pottery-making district around Stoke-on-Trent in Staffordshire, England, where Wedgwood built his factory village and gave it this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Etruscan homeland shares its name with Wedgwood's factory village in Staffordshire's pottery district.

clue.text: Action of a player who doesn't know his own strength

definitions.text: Action of a player who doesn't know his own strength

parts.words: Action of a player who doesn't know his own strength
parts.note: a card player at bridge who bids lower than the hand is worth is failing to value its strength

explanation.surface: An athlete is unaware of how strong they really are.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'player' sounds like a sportsman, but it is a bridge player whose bid is too low for the strength of the cards held.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge, bidding less than a hand deserves is the result of underrating its strength.

clue.text: Evans on 'Change ?

parts.note: 'Change is short for the Stock Exchange; a Mr Evans working there would be a dealer in shares for clients

explanation.surface: A man named Evans is seen on the Stock Exchange floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change, with its apostrophe, is the old short form of the Stock Exchange; the man there buys and sells shares for clients.
explanation.definitionFit: A dealer on the Stock Exchange acts as an agent buying and selling shares for others.

clue.text: The mark of the British fighter

definitions.text: The mark of the British fighter

parts.words: The mark of the British fighter
parts.note: the circular red, white and blue emblem painted on RAF aircraft, including fighter planes

explanation.surface: Something distinguishes the British boxer or soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fighter' suggests a boxer or soldier and 'mark' a quality, but it is a fighter aircraft and the ringed national emblem on its wings.
explanation.definitionFit: The RAF's circular identification disc is a ring-shaped emblem painted on its aircraft.

clue.text: A trifle to shock the Shavians'?

parts.note: a kick is a jolt or sudden shock
Shavians are admirers of George Bernard Shaw, so their man is Shaw

explanation.surface: A small thing is done just to scandalise the admirers of Bernard Shaw.
explanation.walkthrough: To kick Shaw would certainly shock his admirers; the word is an old term for a fancy trinket or dainty dish.
explanation.definitionFit: A kickshaw is a trinket or fancy dish of little value, from French quelque chose.

clue.text: Cape Hasty ?

parts.note: hasty means rash
ness is a word for a headland or cape, found in place-names

explanation.surface: A headland on a map bears the name Hasty.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a place-name, 'Cape Hasty' becomes a headland called Rash, and that headland's name is the quality of being hasty.
explanation.definitionFit: Recklessness or haste is the quality the invented headland's name describes.

clue.text: Rex loads them on a four wheeler

annotationWithheld.why: Rex loads them on a four wheeler (4-4): AXLERODS is an anagram of REX LOADS, but no clue word signals the anagram
annotationWithheld.clue: Rex loads them on a four wheeler

clue.text: Corner-boys, stupid creatures

definitions.meaning: slow pupils once made to stand in the corner of the classroom

explanation.definitionFit: Slow learners, once sent to stand in the classroom corner in pointed caps, are the classic image of stupidity.

clue.text: What's the object of the beauty-class ? Roll-call is the nicest part of it

definitions.text: What's the object of the beauty-class ?

indicators.note: the answer is a part of the words just named, roll-call is the nicest, running across them

explanation.surface: A beauty class's purpose is questioned, and the roll-call is called its best bit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part of it' says the letters run through 'Roll-call is the nicest'. The word comes from Greek kallos, beauty, plus sthenos, strength, so a 'beauty-class' aims at graceful exercise.
explanation.definitionFit: Graceful gymnastic exercise, named from Greek words for beauty and strength, is the aim of such a class.

clue.text: It's more apparent the jumper is successful

definitions.meaning: a jumper who gets over the bar or fence clears it, so is one who clears

explanation.definitionFit: More obvious is the comparative of plain to see, and an athlete who gets over the bar is one who clears it.

clue.text: Writer taking a walk in Oxford

definitions.meaning: Joseph ..., the 18th-century essayist of The Spectator
a riverside path at Magdalen College, Oxford, named after the essayist who was a fellow there

explanation.definitionFit: The Spectator essayist gave his name to the riverside walk at Magdalen College, Oxford, where he studied.

clue.text: No meeting-places here for athletes ?

parts.note: lines that never meet are parallel, and 'meeting-places' also suggests pubs or bars; the gymnast's apparatus has two rails that never meet

explanation.surface: Athletes find nowhere to gather in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: Parallel lines never meet, and a bar is a place to meet for a drink; the gymnastics apparatus is two parallel rails.
explanation.definitionFit: Gymnastic apparatus of two raised rails running side by side, which by geometry never meet.

clue.text: You don't want to join this society

definitions.text: You don't want to join this society

parts.words: You don't want to join this society
parts.note: 'want' means lack: people who lack nothing are rich, so the well-off society is one you join only when you don't want

explanation.surface: A warning to keep away from a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'don't want' reads as a refusal, but 'want' is the old sense of lacking: the rich society is for those who lack nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Wealthy people want for nothing, which is the sense of being well-off or prosperous.

clue.text: Temporarily established at Greenwich ?

parts.note: 'in the interval' is one reading, and the standard time fixed at the Greenwich observatory is the other

explanation.surface: Something is set up at Greenwich for the time being.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Temporarily' hints at 'in the meanwhile', while 'established at Greenwich' points to Greenwich's reference time for the world's clocks.
explanation.definitionFit: The interval between events shares its name with the standard time reckoned from the Greenwich meridian.

clue.text: Alfresco drinks make us a sight better

definitions.meaning: drinking vessels out in the open countryside
binoculars improve our sight of distant things

explanation.walkthrough: 'a sight better' is the idiom for 'much better', but here it is literal: binoculars improve our sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Binoculars for outdoor use improve vision, and 'field' plus 'glasses' reads as drinking vessels used outdoors.

clue.text: Novelist from Warwick

parts.note: Warwick is the first name of the novelist who wrote Sorrell and Son, not the English town

explanation.surface: A writer comes from the English town of Warwick.
explanation.walkthrough: Warwick looks like the county town, but it is the first name of Warwick Deeping, author of Sorrell and Son.
explanation.definitionFit: Warwick Deeping was a popular English novelist of the 1920s and 1930s, best known for Sorrell and Son.

clue.text: Beg for change at ten, round about

indicators.note: round means the scrambled letters go around the piece for about
change tells us to rearrange the letters of at ten

parts.note: re is a short word meaning about or concerning

explanation.surface: Someone pleads for small change at ten o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' looks like coins in the surface, but it is the anagram signal for 'at ten'; 'round' wraps those letters around the short word for 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: To plead earnestly with someone is to beseech or implore them.

clue.text: It was frightful in France before there was a directory

definitions.text: It was frightful in France before there was a directory

parts.words: It was frightful in France before there was a directory
parts.note: the Reign of ... of 1793-94 came before the Directory, the five-man government of revolutionary France

explanation.surface: France had something awful before it got a telephone book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'directory' suggests a phone book, but it is the Directory, the government of France from 1795 that followed the Reign of Terror.
explanation.definitionFit: The period of mass executions in revolutionary France is known as the Reign of Terror.

clue.text: Wagner's Irish bride

parts.note: the Irish princess in Wagner's opera, brought by Tristan to wed King Mark

explanation.surface: The composer Wagner married an Irishwoman.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as Wagner's own wife, but it is the Irish princess of his opera Tristan und Isolde, brought to marry King Mark of Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Tristan und Isolde is an Irish princess promised to King Mark.

clue.text: Light that may be dark

parts.note: a 'dark' type of lamp has a shutter that hides its light

explanation.surface: A source of light that is paradoxically dark.
explanation.walkthrough: The paradox resolves on the 'dark lantern', a lamp with a sliding shutter to hide its beam.
explanation.definitionFit: A lamp in a protective case; the 'dark' kind has a shutter to block the light.

clue.text: Story-book castle

parts.note: ... Castle is the 1931 novel by A. J. Cronin, so the castle of the story-book is the hat-maker's

explanation.surface: A fairy-tale castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Story-book castle' suggests fairy tales, but it is the title of A. J. Cronin's novel Hatter's Castle, minus its second word.
explanation.definitionFit: Cronin's novel Hatter's Castle names a castle belonging to a hat-maker, so the castle's owner word completes the title.

clue.text: She gave her husband a hanky when he wanted one

definitions.text: She gave her husband a hanky when he wanted one

parts.words: She gave her husband a hanky when he wanted one
parts.note: in Othello, Iago's wife hands him Desdemona's handkerchief, which he uses to frame her

explanation.surface: A wife passes her husband a handkerchief when he needs it.
explanation.walkthrough: It sounds like a kind wife, but it is Iago's wife in Shakespeare's Othello, whose gift of Desdemona's handkerchief starts the tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Iago's wife in Othello picks up Desdemona's dropped handkerchief and gives it to him.

clue.text: It's wholly essential

parts.note: the word means both whole or complete and necessary to the whole

explanation.surface: Something is absolutely necessary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wholly essential' reads as 'absolutely needed', but each word is a sense of the answer: whole, and essential.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means forming a necessary part of a whole, and also complete or entire.

clue.text: The hen's dubious antecedent

parts.note: the old puzzle of which came first: the chicken or what it hatched from

explanation.surface: A hen has a questionable ancestor.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'dubious antecedent' is the unanswerable riddle of which came first, the chicken or what it hatched from.
explanation.definitionFit: In the old riddle, the thing a hen hatches from may or may not have come before the hen.

clue.text: No charge, it seems, for the Highlander

definitions.text: No charge, it seems, for the Highlander

parts.words: No charge, it seems, for the Highlander
parts.note: the phrase meaning unpunished or without paying reads as something free for a Scotsman

explanation.surface: A Highlander apparently pays nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scot' was an old tax, so the phrase means untaxed or unpunished; 'it seems' admits the Scotsman link is a play on the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To escape without payment or punishment; scot was an old tax, not a Scotsman.
